html:
On 3 May 1491 Nzinga a Nkuwu, king of Kongo, was baptised by Portuguese priests in his capital Mbanza Kongo. He took the name João I, after the king of Portugal.

Contact had begun when Diogo Cão reached the mouth of the Congo river in 1483. Kongo envoys went to Lisbon and came back with priests, craftsmen and gifts. The king's baptism was a political choice as much as a religious one: it brought a powerful ally and new ritual power.

João I later turned away from the new faith, but his son, baptised as Afonso, made it the state religion when he became king. Kongo stayed Catholic for about four hundred years, in a form that blended Christian saints with Kongo ideas of the spirit world. In the 1700s the prophet Kimpa Vita led a movement that recast the faith in Kongo terms.
